name: ReactOS
summary: Free and open-source operating system designed to provide binary compatibility with the architecture, drivers and Win32 applications of Microsoft Windows NT.
license: Open Source (GNU GPLv2, LGPLv2.1 and BSD licences for some subsystems)

content.introduction: ReactOS is an international free and open-source operating system project aiming to produce a clean and independent clone of the Microsoft Windows NT architecture. Started in 1996 and active for more than two decades, it seeks to let users and enterprises run their software, games and hardware drivers designed for Windows without depending on paid proprietary software or resorting to an application emulation layer.
content.origine_freewin95_et_lancement_de_reacto:
The project originates in a group formed around 1996 under the name FreeWin95, which aimed at a clone of Windows 95 and remained stuck on system design discussion without producing code. At the end of 1997, Jason Filby took over coordination and gathered the still-active subscribers to the mailing list: the target was redirected towards Windows NT and priority given to written code rather than design debates. The project then took the name ReactOS, which the wiki links to dissatisfaction with Microsoft's monopoly on the operating system market, and development began in February 1998.

The early years were slow: few developers knew how to write kernel code, then the basic drivers, notably IDE and keyboard, were added as the kernel stabilised. The wiki states that the code has been written from scratch since 1996 and that the release series run from 0.0.x to 0.4.x, compatibility with Windows Server 2003 being the design goal.
content.what_is_it: Technically, ReactOS is neither a Linux distribution nor a Unix system: it is the only complete and functional reimplementation of the NT kernel architecture developed outside Microsoft's laboratories. It includes a real ring 0 kernel, a hardware abstraction layer (HAL), the `win32k.sys` kernel-space graphics subsystem, as well as a faithful reproduction of the Win32 dynamic libraries (Kernel32, User32, Gdi32) able to load PE/COFF executables natively.
content.kernel_architecture_and_subsystems: The ReactOS kernel faithfully reproduces the internal structure of Windows NT 5.2 (Windows Server 2003 / Windows XP x64), while progressively incorporating programming interfaces introduced in the NT 6.x versions (Windows Vista, 7, 8 and 10). It includes the fundamental executive components: the Object Manager, the process and thread manager, the protected virtual memory manager with hardware paging, the I/O Manager and the Security Reference Monitor (SRM). Hardware drivers compliant with the WDM (Windows Driver Model) model can therefore talk directly to the HAL layer.
content.modele_de_securite_herite_de_nt_et_regla:
The project wiki describes Windows NT as the first mainstream system with a complete implementation of a flexible security model based on access control lists, and links ReactOS to that architecture: system resources, including processes, threads, shared memory segments and the registry, are represented by objects carrying access rights. The same text notes that the permissive default settings of the consumer versions of Windows, retained to ease the transition from Windows 9x, neutralised part of these mechanisms, and states that ReactOS will apply defaults conforming to the model rather than those inherited values.

The provenance of the code is a second documented point: the project FAQ asserts that the developers have not consulted leaked Microsoft source code and rely only on public documentation, including incomplete documentation, which conditions the legality of the reimplementation. The wiki recalls that the code is distributed under GNU GPL 2.0+, some modules under BSD licence.
content.synergy_with_wine_and_userland: To enrich its large Win32 user space without individually rewriting tens of thousands of application APIs, ReactOS maintains a close synergy with the Wine project. ReactOS uses an adapted variant of the Wine dynamic libraries, configured to interface directly with the ReactOS NT kernel through system calls rather than translating requests to the POSIX interface of a Unix kernel. This bidirectional collaboration allows ReactOS to synchronise its multimedia components (DirectX, GDI) regularly, to integrate WineVDM for 16-bit backwards compatibility, and to give Wine its low-level fixes in return.
content.filesystems_and_hardware_drivers: ReactOS supports file systems of the FAT family (FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32) through its internal `fastfat` driver. NTFS file system management is provided for reading and partial writing through a dedicated driver. Innovatively, ReactOS includes the open-source WinBtrfs driver, allowing installation and complete boot of the operating system on partitions formatted in Btrfs with subvolumes and block compression. Device management covers IDE controllers, SATA (AHCI), USB buses and common Ethernet network cards.
content.development_status_and_limitations: Despite significant technical advances and the ability to run popular office software (LibreOffice, Firefox, 7-Zip, VLC) as well as various classic games, ReactOS officially remains at the Alpha development stage (0.4.x series). It must not be considered a complete and stable replacement for Windows for daily production use. Support for recent hardware (USB 3.x controllers, modern Wi-Fi chips, 3D acceleration of recent graphics cards, advanced ACPI sleep) remains partial, and instabilities can occur during intensive multitasking. The system is particularly suited to virtualised environments (QEMU, VirtualBox, VMware) and to older x86 computers.
content.release_0_4_16: Version 0.4.16 was published on 29 August 2026, after about eighteen months of development. It introduces a graphical installer and merges the two historically separate images: the installation bootcd and the test livecd are now one and the same file. The installer offers partition management, file copying and a graphical configuration step. The same version adds improvements to the video, audio, network and storage stacks, as well as a new installation type.
content.driver_stack_and_hardware_support: Release 0.4.16 imports the Kernel-Mode Driver Framework (KMDF), released as open source by Microsoft, to run a new high-definition audio bus driver (sklhdaudbus) that replaces the original unfinished implementation. A new ATA driver replaces UniATA, in use since 2009, and allows booting in generation 1 Hyper-V; a DC21X4 network driver completes hardware coverage. On the memory side, increasing the number of system page table entries removes a slowdown observed with NVIDIA drivers, and ExtEscape was rewritten for AMD drivers. The FastFAT driver imported in 2021 had broken FAT partition repair by chkdsk; the routines have been fixed.
content.wine_api_policy_change: The project abandoned strict conformance to the Windows Server 2003 APIs, which limited it to Wine versions 2.x and 3.x, then began updating its fork towards Wine 10.0. Release 0.4.16 contains a significant part of that work, the migration remaining in progress. Imported third-party components also include the FastFAT driver and elements of the KMDF driver framework, used by the audio stack and the storage stack.
content.installation_types_and_server_core: ReactOS offered two installation types, Workstation and Server, which differ in the graphical options enabled by default. Release 0.4.16 adds Server Core, which disables the Explorer graphical shell while loading the complete Win32 subsystem, on the model of Windows Server Core introduced with Windows Server 2008. This mode is intended for server and embedded use, and differs from the classic Server installation by the absence of a desktop interface.
content.catalogue_de_paquets_rapps_et_depot_rapp:
ReactOS does not embed a dependency manager comparable to APT or RPM: programs are installed by their own installer, and the built-in RAPPS catalogue, formerly Download!, serves to download, install and update them from a single interface. RAPPS resides in `C:\ReactOS\System32` and retrieves its list from the project's public server, in the form of `rappmgr.cab` or `rappmgr2.cab` archives, synchronised on first launch and then extracted into `%appdata%\RApps\appdb` by means of `cabinet.dll`.

Each entry is a text file in INI format, identified by its file name and describing the program through fields such as `Name`, `Category`, `URLDownload`, `RegName`, `SHA1`, `SizeBytes` and `Version`; sections can be declined per language identifier and, in the experimental field set, per architecture. The files are saved in UTF-16 LE with Windows line endings. The catalogue is maintained in the `reactos/rapps-db` repository on GitHub, where additions go through a merge request after a local test in the `appdb` folder.
content.development_model_and_contribution_areas: The site describes the areas open to contributions: system processes (winlogon, lsass, smss, service control manager), shell (shell32.dll, browseui.dll, explorer, in C++ and COM), Win32 API (kernel32.dll, gdi32.dll, user32.dll) and the applications supplied with the system. The tracking tools cited are the GitHub repository, the Jira ticket manager, the Testman testing platform, the wiki, the forum and the mailing lists.
advantages: Native binary compatibility with Win32 applications and Windows NT drivers without a virtualisation layer.
The only complete, free and open reimplementation of the Windows NT kernel existing in the free software world.
Fruitful and continuous synergy with the Wine project for user-space libraries and DirectX.
Native support for the modern Btrfs file system (through WinBtrfs) as the system boot volume.
Very low memory footprint compared with contemporary commercial versions of Windows.
Project under free licences (GNU GPL/LGPL) governed by a non-profit foundation guaranteeing the independence of the code.
disadvantages: Official Alpha status implying occasional system instabilities and a risk of hang or corruption under heavy load.
Limited hardware compatibility on very recent personal computer configurations (Wi-Fi, USB 3, modern GPUs).
Write support on the proprietary NTFS file system remains experimental.
Small development team facing the immensity of the API surface covered by several decades of Windows evolution.
Not suited to a critical enterprise production environment without extensive prior testing.
who_is_it_for: Enthusiasts of software architecture and system developers wishing to explore the inner workings of the Windows NT kernel.
Users wanting to run old professional software or 32-bit Windows games in lightweight virtual machines.
Technicians and maintainers of industrial systems or controllers driven by historical Win32 executables.
Free software advocates and computer security researchers analysing low-level system call mechanisms.
who_is_it_not_for: General public users looking for a primary operating system for their daily work computer.
Modern video game players requiring DirectX 12, advanced Vulkan and recent vendor graphics drivers.
Enterprises looking for a turnkey commercial alternative with contractual guarantees and 24/7 technical support.
Cloud computing server infrastructures requiring Linux container features or cluster high availability.
content.verdict: ReactOS is a free reimplementation of the Windows NT kernel and of the Win32 interface. The project remains in the Alpha phase and is intended for testing, virtualisation and software preservation uses, as well as for the study of Windows system interfaces.

relations.name: Microsoft Windows
relations.note: Proprietary commercial operating system whose NT kernel architecture and Win32 programming interfaces ReactOS reimplements.

relations.name: FreeDOS
relations.note: Free DOS-compatible operating system, sharing with ReactOS the mission of running the historical PC software ecosystem.

relations.name: Haiku
relations.note: Independent free operating system stemming from the legacy of a classic desktop system (BeOS).
